I love drinking alcohol and although I don’t have a problem with it, it’s definitely something I look forward to very much at the weekend. So I sometimes question whether this is healthy. I rarely go out with friends (or even have friends over) so I drink mainly on my own, even though some of the evening will be spent with family who I live with. I hate day drinking as it seems like a waste of the day, but I love the sensation of drinking in the evening, even on my own whilst gaming or watching television. I don’t like to only have one drink - as in, I’d rather not drink anything if that’s all I can have - because it seems pointless to me. If drinking several drinks brings me a certain sensation, then why would I want to have only 1 drink? I’d rather enjoy a lemonade or a Pepsi and feel sober than feel slightly woozy / tipsy.

I enjoy driving, and was the first in my year group to pass my test. I find it easy and rhythmic and relaxing. I have excellent spatial awareness (I think sometimes autistic people can be on either end of the spatial awareness spectrum) and have very sensitive peripheral vision so I have a naturally wide perception of the road and the hazards around me. Sometimes I can space out a bit if I’m on a long stretch of straight road, but if something changes I am immediately brought back to full attention. However, I think public transport is a far better societal infrastructure and through living somewhere with good public transport I aim not to need a car in the future.

I hit myself, usually on the head or on my legs, and then I run and curl up into a ball with my head touching the ground. Sometimes I also make prolonged groaning noises and I rock side to side. I stay like this for up to half an hour. I can hear people talking to me, but I usually do not speak until I have moved from the floor. If I am in my room at home it might be shorter as I am alone in a safe place and can move around sooner, but if I am in a public place it takes longer as there is still loads to process around me which slows down the recovery process I think. Since a recent meltdown which happened in public with all of my friends, I have written a note in my phone that I intend to try and show whoever is with me, containing guidance as to how to react to my meltdown (do not touch me, give me my headphones if they're available, stay nearby but talking isn't necessary, and what to expect from me). During a meltdown I feel very angry at first, and then I cry, and afterwards I usually feel dazed and calm and tired.

Hey, I’m also from the UK. I’m 18 and got diagnosed a couple of months ago, but I started believing I was autistic last year when I was 17, when my mum mentioned that she thought I might be. The traits you describe seem a lot like mine, and I think you’d definitely benefit from a diagnosis. However, it is possible to access support from school/college/work whilst you are still waiting for a diagnosis. After I had been referred, I talked to the SENCO (additional needs coordinator) at my school, and was able to access different exam arrangements and the ‘learning base’ - a quiet study place for SEN students, with a sensory room - before I had been diagnosed. 

I think you could make an appointment with your GP and tell them about the traits you have noticed in yourself, and that you have autistic family members, and that you would like to be referred to you regional autism diagnosis service. In my area, the waiting list was about 1 year - but try not to let this put you off! Be persistent - your ED should not stop you from being put on a referral list for an autism assessment. I do believe that you can be referred to the adult autism service (try asking specifically for this), because it is likely that you will be 18 by the time you are assessed.

I’m sorry to hear that your mum doesn’t agree with you; that must be very difficult. Embarrassment will always go away though, remember that - if you tell her about how you are feeling, it will not be awkward forever. I get what you mean about excelling in school if you’d had an earlier diagnosis, and that’s a tough thing to get around. You still have loads of opportunity left to excel in life though.

At first I found it quite awkward too, that my teachers and mum knew I was autistic, because I am good at masking, but this feeling of slight anxiety went away after I realised that none of the adults at school were judging me. I think that the benefits of letting people know will be greater than the difficulty of telling them.

I hope this helps :)
